paras: The lynching of Sherman Farrior took place in Whiteville, Columbus County, North Carolina, on the night of September 12, 1888, when a body of a hundred or more men took Farrior, a Black prisoner, from the county jail and hanged him from an oak tree. Farrior was awaiting trial on a charge of outraging an aged white woman. North Carolina papers counted the hanging as the thirteenth lynching in the state that year, and reports differed on whether the mob was made up of masked men of unstated race or of Black men.

According to a dispatch from Whiteville printed in the Wilmington Messenger, Farrior was accused of outraging Mrs. E. A. Sasser on August 29. He was given a preliminary hearing before Justices G. W. Fleim and Thos. Barefoot on Monday, September 10, and was committed to jail to await the next term of the Columbus County Superior Court. The same dispatch called him "a man of bad character" who "had repeatedly been engaged in robbery" and said the evidence against him was "conclusive", though it did not say what that evidence was.

On the night of Wednesday, September 12, a body of masked men, "supposed to number a hundred or more", entered the jail and demanded the keys from the jailer. With "a score of revolvers pointed at him", the jailer surrendered the keys, and the men went to Farrior's cell, took him out and left. The next morning his body was found hanging from the limb of a large oak about a mile from the jail. A placard pinned to his breast read "We protect the virtue of our women. Beware!"

No report of an inquest, arrests or a grand-jury inquiry appears in the coverage. The Charlotte Democrat, quoting the Wilmington Star, condemned a recent lynching "in this section of the State" of a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, calling it "the work of negroes". The Star warned that such lynchings would end "in destroying the courts" and called for prompter courts and a jury rule that would let nine men convict; the Democrat added that "It is a terrible thing to execute a man without trial."

The story reached the press as two Raleigh dispatches and a Whiteville dispatch. The first, a Raleigh special of September 14, ran in the Richmond Dispatch under "THE THIRTEENTH. ANOTHER LYNCHING IN THE OLD NORTH STATE. A Negro Brute Hanged", and in the Alexandria Gazette and the Atlanta Constitution. The Raleigh State Chronicle reprinted the Wilmington Messenger's Whiteville account under "A BRUTE LYNCHED", with the placard's words as a subheading. Both of these versions printed, without attribution, the claims that Farrior was of bad character and that the evidence against him was conclusive.

A second Raleigh dispatch, dated September 15, said that "a mob composed of a hundred negroes" had done the hanging, and gave the date of the alleged offense as August 26. Papers outside the South ran that version under headlines stressing the mob's race, such as "A Negro Hung by Colored Men" in the Richmond Daily Times, "Lynched by Colored Men" in the Indianapolis Journal and "A Negro Lynching Bee" in the Rock Island Argus. The St. Paul Globe called him "a Negro Ravisher". Weekly news digests in Chicago and Dakota reduced the story to a single line about a colored man lynched "for assaulting an aged white woman". In North Carolina, the Edenton Fisherman & Farmer noted that the thirteenth lynching of the year "probably breaks the record".

The accounts disagree on who the lynchers were. The Whiteville dispatch, the closest to the scene, and the first Raleigh special describe only "masked men" and give no race. The later Raleigh dispatch says the mob was made up of Black men, and the Wilmington Star's editorial, if it refers to this case, says the same, but neither gives a source for the claim. The reports also differ on the spelling of the names (Farrior or Farrier, Sasser or Sosser), the date of the alleged offense (August 29 or 26) and the wording of the placard.

reader.title: Lynching of Sherman Farrior
bases: A large body of men took a Black prisoner from the Whiteville jail by force and hanged him from a tree (A1, A3, A8).

Farrior was taken from jail by a hundred or more men who forced the jailer to give up the keys and was found hanged (A1, A3, A8); he was awaiting trial on a charge of outraging a white woman, and the placard on his body, 'We protect the virtue of our women,' stated the mob's pretext (A1, A8).

A Wilmington Messenger dispatch from Whiteville (A8) and two separate Raleigh dispatches (A1, A3) agree that a hundred or more men took Farrior from the jail and hanged him, though they disagree on who the men were.

accounts.label: Wilmington Star editorial
